opus-5.5.text:
I think we're at a kind of halftime moment.

For roughly the past decade, the first half of AI was about methods and models. People came up with new training techniques and architectures, like the Transformer, pre-training, and RL algorithms. Then they showed progress by climbing benchmarks. If you had a better method, you got a higher score on ImageNet or some language benchmark, you wrote a paper, and that was the game. The intellectual excitement was mostly on the method side, and benchmarks were treated as something you just pick up and beat.

What changed is that we now have something like a general recipe. It's large-scale pre-training, plus reasoning, plus reinforcement learning, and the models can act through language and tools. Once you have that, the recipe tends to solve benchmarks very quickly. A new benchmark comes out, and within months it's saturated. So the old loop of "new method, higher score" is losing its meaning. The bottleneck is no longer only "can we build a smarter model?" It's more "what problems should we actually be solving, and how do we measure real progress?"

So in this second half, I think evaluation and problem definition become as important as training, maybe more. There's an awkward gap. Models are already superhuman on many exams and competitions, but the economic and real-world impact isn't proportional to that yet. Part of the reason is that our evaluations assume things that don't match reality. They assume tasks are independent and run automatically, while real work is interactive, with humans in the loop, and long-horizon, where you accumulate context and experience over time.

So for me, today's stage is that the capability is largely there and the recipe works. The next phase is about utility: building agents that do useful things in real environments, figuring out the right settings and metrics, and turning intelligence into products and value. That requires thinking a bit more like a product person or a researcher defining new problems, not just someone optimizing a number on a leaderboard.

r001.rationale: The response says the bottleneck has shifted from building a smarter model to deciding what problems to solve and how to measure progress, including whether evaluations match real tasks.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Gemini, OpenAI, or Anthropic, or say they no longer worry about catching up with one another.

fable-5.1.text:
I think we're at a halftime. That's actually the phrase I used in a blog post I wrote, "The Second Half." If you look at the history of AI over the past several decades, the first half was really about developing new methods and new models. You had different architectures, different training approaches, and the field progressed by inventing better ways to train things. Transformers, pretraining, RLHF, chain-of-thought, and so on. Benchmarks were mostly there to measure whether the new method worked.

What's changed is that we've now found a recipe that generalizes. Pretraining on massive data, plus reasoning through language, plus reinforcement learning on top of that. Once you have that recipe, you can throw almost any task at it, whether it's math, coding, or agent tasks, and it just keeps getting better. The method is no longer the bottleneck.

So the second half is about a different question. It's not "how do we train the model," it's "what should we train it to do, and how do we know it's actually useful?" That means defining the right tasks, building the right environments, and designing evaluations that reflect real-world value rather than something artificial. Our benchmarks keep getting saturated, and yet the economic impact lags behind. That gap tells you the evaluation setup is wrong, not that the models are too weak.

A concrete example: most benchmarks are i.i.d., every problem is independent, and the model starts fresh each time. But real work isn't like that. A human doing a job accumulates context, learns from previous interactions, deals with the same user over a long horizon. Our evaluations mostly don't test for that. So I think the next stage is less about a bigger model and more about rethinking the problem setup, with the right environments, the right priors, and reinforcement learning that actually generalizes.

In short, I'd say the hard science problem of "how to make intelligence" has been largely solved in recipe form. The remaining problem is more like an engineering and product problem, which is in some ways harder because it requires taste about what matters.

r001.rationale: The response says the training method is no longer the bottleneck and shifts focus to defining useful tasks and evaluations, which communicates the move from whether AI can perform a task to whether the task is well defined.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Gemini, OpenAI, or Anthropic, or express a view about whether they worry about catching up with one another.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re at a transition from AI that can answer questions to AI that can actually carry out tasks. Those sound similar, but there’s a substantial gap between them. Giving a useful answer is one thing; taking actions, observing what happens, recovering from mistakes, and completing a longer task is another.

So when we ask what stage AI has reached, I’d separate capability from reliability. A model might solve a very difficult problem in one interaction and then fail on something fairly simple in another. That makes it hard to describe progress with a single label, like whether it has reached human intelligence.

For me, the interesting question is how much responsibility we can delegate to it. Can it help with one step? Can it complete a task with supervision? Can it work independently and recognize when it needs to ask for help? We’re moving along that spectrum, but unevenly.

That’s why I see this as a very promising stage, but also one where there’s a lot of work between an impressive demonstration and something people can depend on.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from AI answering questions to carrying out tasks, and emphasizes reliability. It does not say the concern has shifted from whether AI can perform a task to whether the task is well defined.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Gemini, OpenAI, Anthropic, or their concerns about catching up with one another.

sol-6.1.text:
我觉得我们现在处在一个挺有意思的转折点：AI 正在从一个“能回答问题的模型”，变成一个“能完成任务的系统”。以前大家更多关注，你问它一道题，它能不能答对；现在我们开始关心，给它一个目标，它能不能自己拆解问题、使用工具、根据反馈调整，最后把事情做完。

这两者之间其实还有很大的距离。回答问题，你可能只需要生成一次答案；完成任务，你需要连续做很多决策。哪怕每一步成功率都挺高，整个过程拉长以后，也很容易出错。所以我觉得，今天我们一方面看到了很强的能力，另一方面也看到了这些能力在真实环境里的不稳定性。

对我来说，接下来一个很重要的问题是：怎么把模型的智能，变成可靠、可验证、真正对人有用的行动能力。这不只是把模型做大，也涉及它怎么和环境交互，怎么发现自己错了，以及什么时候应该停下来问人。我们已经看到这个方向的可能性，但距离成熟还有很多工作要做。

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from answering questions to completing tasks, then discusses reliability and verification. It does not say that concern has shifted from task performance to whether the task is well defined.
